text:
An agent running bad content just hands you bad content faster.

Automation multiplies whatever quality you already have. It never creates quality you don't.

People keep asking me the difference between a skill and an agent.

A skill is a recipe. You write it once and it runs the same every time.

An agent is the thing that runs the recipe while you're not looking.

The recipes don't cook, the agents cook.

The mistake I see with agents right now: people automate everything while everything is still sitting at about 60%.

I do the opposite.

I only hand an agent something that's already really good.

If a skill still needs my corrections every time, it isn't ready to be an agent yet.

Two kinds of agents, two completely different bars:

- Trigger agents: someone replies, connect them here. You can't really do this wrong, so automate it today.
- Quality agents: writing your posts, your emails. These only work if the work is already good.

Point a quality agent at weak work and you just ship weak work faster.

The first agent I'm installing checks Notion, TLDV, Drive and Slack before it proposes anything.

Then it writes the blocks straight into my calendar.

I don't touch it.

A skill still needs me sitting there. An agent runs while I'm gone.

What I like about building with AI is it's cumulative.

You build one skill, then another, then another.

None of it resets. The folders just keep growing, and every week the engine does a little more of the work for you.

My whole content week is two moves.

An analysis on Monday.

Then the entire week of content produced in a couple of hours.

The system does the heavy lifting, I make the calls on what ships.

I'm keeping all my writing manual on purpose.

I could automate it. I don't, because I correct it constantly and the algorithm keeps changing under my feet.

The day I stop correcting the writing is the day it earns an agent.

Not before.

Going from doing content by hand to letting AI run it creates some disparities.

Things break in ways you don't notice right away.

Usually it's because you didn't give it enough context, so it quietly does something you didn't expect.

That's the cost of the switch. Worth paying, but nobody warns you about it.

Agents bought me back about 30 minutes a day.

Small on paper.

But I don't spend those 30 minutes relaxing, I spend them building the next agent.

That's how it compounds. You save time, then spend the saved time saving more.

The quiet win from agents nobody talks about.

I stopped holding the backlog in my head.

The stuff that's easy to ignore and easy to forget just gets done now, whether I remember it or not.

If you want to move your content from AI-assisted to AI-run, start here:

- Automate the mechanical stuff first. Triggers, connections, the "check these four tools before proposing anything" jobs.
- Leave your writing alone until it stops needing your corrections.

Do it in that order and you won't blow up the part that carries your voice.

If your tweets have always been ass, an agent won't fix them.

It'll just post ass on schedule.

Get the work good first. Automate second.

I've built five, six, maybe seven lead magnet formats already:

- Notion
- Canva
- Gamma
- a PDF
- raw HTML

The formats keep changing because the algorithm keeps changing.

That's exactly why I won't hand this part to an agent yet. A moving target needs my feedback in the loop.

The agents I actually want aren't the ones that tidy my calendar.

They're the ones that go get calls.

Qualified calls with real buyers, not calls with people who are just learning about AI.

That's the version of this that changes the business, and it's what I'm building toward.

Early on my whole system was ChatGPT projects and a pile of the same chat sessions.

It worked, sort of.

Now it's skills in a repo, moving toward agents that run on their own on weekdays.

Same idea the whole way through: stop rewriting the prompt from scratch every single time.

The loop that gets a skill ready for an agent:

I run it. I correct what's off. The skill updates so it won't make that mistake again.

Repeat until I stop correcting it.

When the corrections dry up, it's agent-ready. That's the only signal I trust.

The bar for automating something isn't "can an agent do this."

It's "is this already good enough that I'd ship it without looking."

A lot of what people are rushing to automate fails that test.

Fix the work. Then let it run.
